practice_items.prompt: A firewall examines each packet independently without remembering previous packets. Which type is this?
practice_items.explain: A stateless (packet-filter) firewall evaluates each packet in isolation using only header fields, with no memory of prior packets or connections.

practice_items.prompt: Which data structure does a stateful firewall use to recognize legitimate return traffic?
practice_items.explain: The connection-tracking table records active sessions (source/destination IP, ports, protocol, state). Return packets matching an established entry are automatically permitted.

practice_items.prompt: Select ALL fields a stateless packet-filter firewall can use in its rules.
practice_items.explain: Stateless firewalls operate on header fields: source/destination IP, port numbers, and protocol. They cannot inspect TCP connection state because they track no state.

practice_items.prompt: An attacker sends a TCP packet with the ACK flag set, spoofing a session that was never established. A stateful firewall will:
options: Forward it because ACK packets are always allowed
Drop it because no matching session exists in the connection-tracking table
Forward it because the destination port matches a permit rule
Drop it because ACK packets are never allowed inbound
practice_items.explain: A stateful firewall checks whether the packet belongs to a tracked session. An ACK for a session not in the table is dropped as an unsolicited or spoofed packet.

practice_items.prompt: Name the three-packet exchange that a stateful firewall uses to detect the start of a legitimate TCP connection.
practice_items.explain: The TCP three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) establishes a connection. Stateful firewalls track this sequence to know when a session is legitimately open.

practice_items.prompt: Which scenario BEST justifies using a stateless firewall instead of a stateful one?
options: High-throughput edge router where simple IP/port rules and raw speed are the priority
Protecting an internal database server from spoofed packets
Filtering encrypted HTTPS traffic for malware
Tracking which users are currently logged in to the network
practice_items.explain: Stateless firewalls excel where raw throughput matters and simple permit/deny rules are sufficient, such as high-speed edge routers. Richer inspection requires stateful or application-layer firewalls.

practice_items.atom_title: Firewall rules and access control lists (ACLs)
practice_items.prompt: A firewall ACL evaluates a packet against its rule list. Which rule's action is applied?
options: The rule with the most specific source address
The first rule (top to bottom) that matches
practice_items.explain: ACLs use first-match-wins: evaluation stops at the first rule whose conditions match the packet, regardless of any later rules that might also match.

practice_items.atom_title: Firewall rules and access control lists (ACLs)
practice_items.prompt: A packet reaches the bottom of an ACL without matching any explicit rule. What happens?
options: It is dropped by the implicit deny
It is queued for manual review
practice_items.explain: A well-formed ACL ends with an implicit (or explicit) deny-all rule. Unmatched traffic is dropped by default.

practice_items.atom_title: Firewall rules and access control lists (ACLs)
practice_items.prompt: Select ALL fields a typical ACL rule matches on.
practice_items.explain: ACL rules match header fields: source, destination, port, and protocol. Inspecting payload content is beyond a basic ACL (that is application-layer inspection).

practice_items.atom_title: Firewall rules and access control lists (ACLs)
practice_items.prompt: An admin places 'allow TCP any any port 22' as rule 1, then 'deny TCP 203.0.113.0 to 10.0.1.10 port 22' as rule 4. What happens to traffic from 203.0.113.0 to port 22?
options: It is denied, because rule 4 is more specific
The firewall evaluates both rules and denies since deny takes priority
It is allowed, because rule 1 matches first and rule 4 is shadowed
It depends on which rule was written most recently
practice_items.explain: Rule 1 is broader and matches first, so its allow action applies. Rule 4 is unreachable (shadowed) for that traffic, specificity does not override rule order.

practice_items.atom_title: Firewall rules and access control lists (ACLs)
practice_items.prompt: Name the anomaly where a broad rule earlier in an ACL makes a more specific rule below it unreachable.
practice_items.explain: Rule shadowing: an earlier, broader-matching rule prevents a later, more specific rule from ever being evaluated.

practice_items.atom_title: Firewall rules and access control lists (ACLs)
practice_items.prompt: What is the safest general pattern for ordering ACL rules?
options: Broadest allow rules first, specific denies last
Most specific rules (denies/exceptions) first, general allows next, implicit deny-all last
Order does not matter if the rule set is small
practice_items.explain: Placing specific exceptions and denies before general allow rules prevents shadowing and keeps the default-deny posture intact.
